newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Rights group slams violations in Kabila's Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Rights group slams violations in Kabila's Kinshasa.

text.p: The main human rights watchdog in Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo has denounced summary executions and other violations by his forces in the capital and expressed concern about prospects for democracy.

The Association for the Defence of Human Rights (AZADHO) report, which focused on Kinshasa, coincided with U.N. efforts to investigate allegations of massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees by Kabila's soldiers or Rwandan Tutsi allies in eastern Zaire.
"The AZADHO has noted with concern a slide by the new authorities towards a totalitarian state," it said.

The report, published in Kinshasa, put the death toll just before, during and after the May 17 fall of the city at 647 and described soldiers of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) as trigger-happy.

"Members of the AFDL have shown themselves to be trigger-happy which resulted in carnage -- 647 people have been shot dead in Kinshasa and on the road to Bandundu," it said, referring to the main approach road to Kinshasa.

AZADHO also denounced treatment of young women who had been stripped and beaten by Kabila's soldiers for wearing mini-skirts or tight trousers and appealed to the international community to link aid to human rights in Africa's third largest nation.
The report focused on the period since Kabila toppled veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko on May 17 and declared himself president of the former Zaire.
Kabila, whose forces won a seven-month civil war, has given himself sweeping powers and banned political activity but has promised elections by April 1999.
The report said moves towards democracy were threatened by the ban. It said abuses highlighted in the report had been reported by AZADHO activists and volunteers of the local Red Cross.
"The AZADHO has noticed that the AFDL and its armed forces are acting as courts and tribunals," it said, adding that Kabila's soldiers were behaving like those from Mobutu's army.
It said those summarily executed included soldiers of Mobutu's defeated army, looters and innocent civilians.
AZADHO said that 269 bodies, of which 80 were burned and mutilated, were buried in mass graves in May at the cemetery of Mikonga, in the eastern suburb of the sprawling capital city.
"More than 100 decomposing bodies have been dumped on the plateau of Bateke" outside Kinshasa on the way to the Bandundu Province, it added.
The AZADHO report said AFDL soldiers had inflicted cruel or inhuman treatment on a number of people.
Kabila's administration, while frowning on the wearing of mini-skirts or tight trousers, has said they are not banned and has condemned attacks on girls wearing them by its soldiers.

AZADHO expressed concern about the fate of 16 members of the former Rwandan Hutu army. The Rwandan Hutu troops joined an exodus of Rwandan Hutus to Mobutu's Zaire after being blamed for the genocide of hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis there in 1994. Many fought alongside Mobutu's army in the civil war.

AZADHO said the 16 were were taken in May from Kinshasa's Mama Yemo hospital where they were receiving treatment to the AFDL-controlled Camp Mobutu in Kinshasa's Lemba district and had not been seen since.
Kabila has agreed to a U.N. probe of the massacre allegations in the east. The two sides are still trying to agree implementation details.
